nameStory: The reddish brown sea cucumber gets its straightforward name from its distinctive rusty-brown coloration and its cucumber-like shape when relaxed. Despite being called the 'reddish brown' sea cucumber, it's also known as the orange-footed sea cucumber due to its bright orange tube feet that extend like tiny fingers from its body.
description: This is New England's largest sea cucumber - a soft, elongated marine animal that looks like a living, breathing pickle on the ocean floor. When fully extended, it has a cylindrical body with a leathery, bumpy texture that feels somewhat like wet rubber. The creature uses branching, feathery tentacles around its mouth to filter tiny particles from the water for food. It's one of the most common sea cucumbers you'll encounter in New England's cold coastal waters.

idTips.label: Body color and texture
idTips.description: Distinctive reddish-brown to dark brown leathery skin with a bumpy, warty texture that feels firm but yielding when gently touched

idTips.label: Orange tube feet
idTips.description: Bright orange tube feet extend from the underside like tiny suction cups, creating striking color contrast against the dark body

idTips.label: Feeding tentacles
idTips.description: Ten branching, feathery tentacles around the mouth that look like tiny trees and can quickly retract when disturbed

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: Cucumber-shaped body that can stretch and contract dramatically, being New England's largest sea cucumber species

idTips.label: Movement response
idTips.description: Contracts into a firm, shortened mass when touched or startled, then slowly extends again when left undisturbed

habitat: Found in New England's cold coastal waters from the intertidal zone down to deeper waters, typically on rocky bottoms, kelp beds, or among eelgrass. They prefer areas with good water circulation where they can filter-feed effectively. Look for them attached to rocks, pilings, or nestled among seaweed during low tide explorations.

seasonality.spring: Becomes more active as waters warm, with feeding tentacles more frequently extended. Good time to observe them in tide pools as they begin their peak feeding season.
seasonality.summer: Most active period with tentacles fully extended for feeding. Easiest to spot and identify during summer low tides when they're actively filter-feeding.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to slow down as water temperatures drop. Their reddish-brown coloration may appear more pronounced against dying seaweed.
seasonality.winter: Less active in coldest months, often contracted and harder to spot. May appear more like dark rocks when tightly contracted in winter tide pools.

funFact: When severely stressed or attacked, sea cucumbers can actually eject their internal organs through their mouth or rear end and then regenerate them completely over several months - it's like throwing your lunch at a predator and then growing a new stomach!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other dark, blob-like marine creatures when contracted, but the orange tube feet are a dead giveaway. Remember: 'Orange feet, reddish treat' - no other New England sea cucumber has such bright orange tube feet against a dark body.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name 'sea cucumber,' these animals are echinoderms, more closely related to sea stars and sea urchins than to any plant. The cucumber comparison comes purely from their shape and bumpy skin texture, similar to how a pickle looks.
compareHints: As New England's largest sea cucumber and the only common Cucumaria species in our waters, it stands out from smaller, smoother sea cucumber species by its substantial size, distinctly bumpy texture, and bright orange tube feet. Other regional sea cucumbers tend to be smaller, smoother, and lack the dramatic color contrast between body and feet.
